title: Hamlet
author: William Shakespeare
openingChapterLabel: Act I, Scene I — Elsinore. A platform before the castle.
openingText: BERNARDO: Who's there? FRANCISCO: Nay, answer me. Stand and unfold yourself. BERNARDO: Long live the King! FRANCISCO: Bernardo? BERNARDO: He. FRANCISCO: You come most carefully upon your hour. BERNARDO: 'Tis now struck twelve. Get thee to bed, Francisco. FRANCISCO: For this relief much thanks. 'Tis bitter cold, and I am sick at heart.
about: Hamlet's father is dead. His uncle has married his mother and taken the throne. A ghost appears and demands revenge. The play is about why Hamlet doesn't simply act — and whether the thinking that stops him is a weakness or the only sane response to an impossible situation.

angleCards.title: Mad or performing madness?
angleCards.text: Hamlet tells Horatio he will put on an "antic disposition." But by Act IV it is less clear who is in control. Notice when his behaviour serves a strategic purpose — and when it seems to have slipped the leash.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read Hamlet as a study in madness — whether his is real or performed, and what the difference tells us about sanity itself.

angleCards.title: The problem of acting under uncertainty.
angleCards.text: Everyone else in the play — Claudius, Laertes, Fortinbras — acts decisively. Hamlet thinks. The play takes his thinking seriously rather than dismissing it. Ask what he actually knows, and when.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to understand why Hamlet cannot act — what stops him when every other character in the play seems to know exactly what to do.

angleCards.title: Revenge vs. justice.
angleCards.text: The ghost demands Hamlet kill Claudius. But Hamlet wants more than death — he wants punishment that fits the crime, guilt that is witnessed. That distinction drives every delay in the play.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read this as a meditation on revenge versus justice — why revenge feels demanded but keeps being deferred.

angleCards.title: Thinking too much.
angleCards.text: "Thus conscience does make cowards of us all." Hamlet says it himself. But the play is not sure it agrees. Watch whether his reflectiveness is a flaw or a form of moral seriousness that the world he lives in cannot accommodate.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to trace the relationship between overthinking and paralysis — whether Hamlet's intelligence is his greatest asset or the thing that destroys him.

cast.name: Hamlet
cast.description: Thirty years old, a student at Wittenberg, home for his father's funeral. He is the most intelligent person in every room he enters — and it nearly destroys him.

cast.name: Claudius
cast.description: Hamlet's uncle, now king and stepfather. He killed his brother and took everything. He is not a cartoon villain — he has genuine political skill and, in private, something resembling a conscience.

cast.name: Gertrude
cast.description: Queen of Denmark, recently remarried. The play keeps her inner life deliberately opaque — we never know how much she knows. That ambiguity is the point.

cast.name: Ophelia
cast.description: Polonius's daughter, Hamlet's former intimacy. She is caught between the demands of the men around her with no room to manoeuvre. Her arc is the play's most quietly devastating.

cast.name: Horatio
cast.description: Hamlet's university friend, the one person he trusts completely. He survives the play because Hamlet asks him to — so the story can be told. He is the reader's surrogate.

cast.name: The Ghost
cast.description: Hamlet's father, or something wearing his face. He appears, names his murderer, and demands revenge. Whether he should be trusted is one of the play's central questions.
